Why Paper Still Wins

By Grace Hopper

Reading on paper has a quality that screens have struggled to match. The page stays still, the light is reflected rather than emitted, and nothing competes for your attention while you follow an argument from one paragraph to the next.

E-ink devices close much of that gap. They reflect ambient light, hold a page without refreshing, and let you write in the margins with a stylus. For long-form articles they are a natural fit, provided the article can be moved off the web and onto the device.

The remaining friction is getting text there. Copying, pasting and converting by hand works once, but a reading habit needs something closer to a single tap: share a link, and the article simply appears on the device a few moments later.

That is the whole idea. Everything else is detail about extraction, formatting and synchronisation.
